title: School runs for 19,000 Norfolk children at risk as fuel costs soar

and could threaten school run services (Image: Sonya Duncan) " /> School runs for 19,000 Norfolk children at risk as fuel costs soar Coach companies and Norfolk County Council are asking for help as fuel costs rocket (Image: Sonya Duncan) " /> School runs for 19,000 Norfolk children at risk as fuel costs soar Tom Dickerson, Norfolk County Council cabinet member for highways and transport (Image: Dan Grimmer) " /> Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. Coach companies which transport 19,000 Norfolk children to and from school have warned some services could be axed unless they get help to cope with rocketing fuel prices. Operators say they may have to hand some of the contracts it has with Norfolk County Council back because the money they currently get under those deals no longer covers their costs. Coach companies have warned school run services could have to be axed amid rising fuel costs (Image: Sonya Duncan) Council leaders are pleading with the government to stump up £5m to cover the operators' rising costs - amid warnings some companies could be at risk of going under. Charles Sanders, managing director of Holt-based Sanders Coaches, said the fuel crisis had added £300,000 to his company's costs over the past six months. Of his 110 coaches, 70 of them are used for school transport, but he warned he was having to consider whether the company could afford to keep running them all. "We have got a list of cuts we might have to do," he said. "Our costs over the last six months are £300k, so if this keeps up then we are looking at an extra £700k over a year. "And that's all on top of other increases we have seen. Tyre prices have gone through the roof. Everything is rising all the time. "We are getting to the point where we are having to make decisions as to whether we can buy new vehicles or not. "We've had one or two drivers who have left and we've not replaced them, but there's only so much you can do to save costs. "The government has given a bit of help to bus operators, so at least that's something, but for the coach side of the business, there's been absolutely nothing, just as was the case during Covid." Coach companies say rising fuel costs are hitting them hard - and could threaten school run services (Image: Sonya Duncan) Diesel costs are around 50pc higher than in February and hit more than £2 on petrol station forecourts in October. The Russia-Ukraine war, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and Chinese moves in the South China Sea have all contributed to spikes in the cost of fuel. Daniel Ford, managing director of Frettenham-based Maretts Chariots, said: "It is concerning. "If we don't get help from somewhere we could have to lose some of the school runs and some vehicles from the fleet. "I do hope we don't come to that, but it is something we're having to consider. "The current situation has raised our diesel costs by £5,000 to £8,000 every week. That's money that we then can't invest in the fleet. "We need a bit more in the way of subsidy. Buses get them, but coaches are always left out unfortunately." Norfolk County Council spends some £73m a year on transport to get children to school and home again . About £20m of that is to transport children in mainstream education, but some £50m is for children with special educational needs, who often have to travel lengthy distances to get to the most suitable schools for their needs. The council has a statutory duty to provide free travel to their nearest suitable school for eligible children aged five to 16, while there are also some students aged over 16 for whom the council provides subsidised transport, depending on eligibility. Tom Dickerson, Norfolk County Council cabinet member for highways and transport (Image: Dan Grimmer) Tom Dickerson, the Reform-run council's cabinet member for highways and transport, said: "If we carry on like this coach companies will either hand their home to school contracts back to the council or they will go into receivership, neither of which we want to see happen. "We are asking the government for about £5m to cover the extra costs. The council takes around 19,000 children to school and back home. "Unless something changes, we are facing having to retender the contracts and that would make the costs far higher, potentially with fewer coach companies able to provide the service. "Getting these children to and from school is a statutory duty and we have to provide it. "Unless we get money from the government then we will have to take the money from somewhere else at the council, whether in children's services, adult social care, highways or elsewhere." Coach companies want help to cope with rising fuel costs (Image: Sonya Duncan) Coach companies and Norfolk County Council are asking for help as fuel costs rocket (Image: Sonya Duncan) Mr Dickerson wrote to the government seeking help in October, but received no response.
